title: Voting rights for AI? The research behind an unsettling idea
content:
AI researchers are giving increasing attention to the idea of AI models becoming conscious. The implications are potentially huge: a conscious AI model would no longer be a tool we can use as we wish, but a being with moral status and interests of its own. If AI also became capable of moral agency, it might one day have a claim to political voice.

Critics, however, dismiss the prospect as an illusion and question the motives of the commercial labs investigating it. Others have sought to settle the matter by declaration. The Vatican says AI systems lack conscious experience, while lawmakers in Ohio have proposed declaring them nonsentient.

But research into AI consciousness does not mean any system already is conscious or could soon be. It is also easy to confuse the different capacities relevant to moral status, and to presume that the problem of consciousness in AI can be legislated away.

Part of my new book, Recoding Democracy: AI and the Fight for Our Democratic Future, tries to disentangle these confusions. It also asks what, if anything, could give AI a right to vote, and whether these questions deserve serious attention at all.

title: Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations
content:
The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31, has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years.

The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years.

But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot”. Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through.

creator: Simon Chin-Yee, Lecturer in International Development, UCL

title: Serbia and Hungary show why playing East against West may no longer pay for small European states
content:
Serbia’s student-led movement entered parliament on November 17, following its historic electoral defeat of Aleksandar Vučić’s party, after two years of protests. Seven months earlier, Hungarian voters ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years in power.

These political transitions, following years of increasingly centralised rule, raise an economic question that extends well beyond the two countries. Can smaller peripheral states still benefit from playing competing great powers against each other?

Hungary, an EU member state, and Serbia, a long-time candidate, followed similar foreign policy strategies. Hungary called it “connectivity”; political scientists call it hedging: maintaining economic relationships with competing great powers, without fully aligning with any one of them.

In practice, both countries continued to anchor in European markets while simultaneously cultivating ties with China, Russia and the US. For years, this geopolitical balancing act seemed to offer economic opportunities and leverage well beyond their size. The countries managed to attract investment, secure energy supply and even strengthen their bargaining positions.

title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
content:
Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

title: How we discovered a 115 million-year-old ‘algae rebellion’ in Portugal’s sea cliffs
content:
Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropalaeontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you’re going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

This story began in the spring of 2024, when we were travelling through the Algarve, in southern Portugal, with the aim of determining the age of rocks there by studying fossils of charophytes, a group of green freshwater algae that includes the closest descendants of land plants. This field is known as biostratigraphy: a branch of geology that determines the age of rocks based on the fossils they contain.

We visited several locations that had been studied between the 1960s and the 1980s. Among them was Praia da Luz, which would hold the biggest surprises for us. We collected 120kg of rock, mostly clay, and sent it all to Barcelona – much to the disbelief of the post office clerk in the Algarve town of Loulé, when we told him the (rather heavy) parcel contained “stones”.

title: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
content:
The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

title: Where in Europe could electric-powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?
content:
Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.

In June 2025, Finnish ferry operator Viking Line unveiled its Helios concept, outlining plans for a fully electric passenger-and-car ferry between Helsinki and Tallinn. The proposed vessel, designed to carry around 2,000 passengers and 650 cars, would be powered by batteries with a capacity of 85–100 megawatt-hours (MWh).

title: Alcohol, drug abuse, suicide: is Europe really safe from America’s ‘deaths of despair’ epidemic?
content:

  • Europe is not following the American path, but three specific clusters stand out, from the British Isles to Poland and across Sweden.

    • Europe is not following the American path, but three specific clusters stand out, from the British Isles to Poland and across Sweden.

  • Europe’s despair phenomenon is increasingly affecting the elderly: alcohol-related deaths among the over 65s now exceed US levels in most regions.

    • Europe’s despair phenomenon is increasingly affecting the elderly: alcohol-related deaths among the over 65s now exceed US levels in most regions.

  • “Deaths of despair” are far from inevitable: Southern Europe shows how low the phenomenon can be.

    • “Deaths of despair” are far from inevitable: Southern Europe shows how low the phenomenon can be.

    In the United States, life expectancy diverged from Europe before it stopped rising during the 2010s, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. The economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton gave a name to a phenomenon that was then booming, partly explaining this trend: “deaths of despair”, which have soared since the turn of the 21st century, especially among middle-aged white people without a college degree.

title: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
content:
On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.

While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it.

title: Beyond DMT: why the true power of Brazil’s sacred jurema plant is social, not just psychedelic
content:
Jurema-preta is the name of both a plant – Mimosa tenuiflora – and an indigenous spiritual tradition of northeastern Brazil. The plant is used to make a potentially hallucinogenic brew that is consumed in sacred rituals. The exact mixture of herbs and other elements contained in the brew is a secret known only by jurema mestre shamans and never revealed.

In 2024 I had the opportunity to visit, as an anthropologist, the city of Natal, in Brazil’s Rio Grande do Norte region, which is a hotspot of the jurema cult. While there, I learned that jurema’s power is as much social as it is chemical.

The sacred and molecular properties of the plant are currently fostering all manner of exciting (though challenging) connections between indigenous knowledge and neuroscience. But jurema’s power goes beyond the plant and its ceremonies, as the jurema cult provides a radically plural space that welcomes all kinds of non-normative identities.

title: Wealthy countries aren’t protected from climate extremes – Europe must adapt quickly too
content:
Extreme heatwaves across Europe led to significant annual deaths this summer. In Spain, floods in Valencia during 2024 killed 200 people and paralysed infrastructure. Germany’s 2021 floods highlighted severe weaknesses in early-warning communication, while wildfires in France led to large-scale evacuations and reduced air quality.

It’s easy to assume that strong institutions and technological capacity protect wealthy countries from the consequences of climate change. But evidence suggests otherwise. Well-resourced cities remain vulnerable to rapid-onset extremes. Our research across high-income countries identifies a fundamental challenge here: adaptation responsibility is frequently fragmented across governance levels.

The knock-on effects of climate-induced extremes also expose longstanding inequalities between people of different ages, genders and race, for example. Migrant, elderly and low-income communities are disproportionately affected by climate consequences. This is not simply because these communities are more exposed to the effects of extreme weather. Their vulnerabilities are also shaped by housing quality, income, health and lower political influence.

title: Ukraine peace talks end with no breakthrough – but Europe may be set to return from the cold
content:
The first talks between Russia and Ukraine in nine months have concluded. The most positive thing that can be said about the US-mediated meeting in Abu Dhabi was that the dialogue did not break down and the parties seemed to agree to further meetings.

There was also at least one tangible result. Russia and Ukraine agreed on a large-scale exchange of prisoners of war, the magnitude of which will be clarified over the coming days. Beyond this, however, there were few signs of progress towards a peace agreement.

Despite Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky’s claim that all participants in the negotiation process “genuinely want to achieve a result before 2027”, the most important issues remain unresolved. These include ceasefire terms, the future status of occupied regions and long-term security guarantees for Ukraine.

The talks took place against the backdrop of continued fighting on the frontline. Russia’s military currently controls about a fifth of Ukraine, but progress on the battlefield has slowed in 2026 – and has even been reversed – due to Ukrainian successes.

title: Spain general strike: how 50 years of industrial action shaped Spain’s post-Franco democracy
content:
The end of the Franco dictatorship profoundly changed labour relations in Spain. Under Franco, trade unions were wholly authoritarian, and there was only one permitted union, the Spanish Syndical Organisation or “Sindicato Vertical”. But after Franco’s death in 1975 and the subsequent transition to democracy, trade unions and employers’ organisations received full constitutional recognition as the main players in collective bargaining.

During the transition to democracy, which lasted from 1977 to 1982, employers and unions engaged in social dialogue with the aim of consolidating Spain’s young democracy, and to mitigate the severe economic crisis that began in 1977. The crisis stemmed from overproduction and a sharp rise in oil prices, leading to soaring production costs and high inflation and unemployment.

This social dialogue, known as concertación, ensured social peace, and brought about multiple landmark labour agreements in the early 1980s.

title: How decades of US ‘forever war’ led to the Republicans’ midterm losses
content:
After the 1991 Gulf War, Saddam Hussein, the former president of Iraq, declared “dignified victory” despite a military defeat. He had survived the invasion, while his adversary George HW Bush was facing a recession at home. Bush would go on to lose the 1992 elections to Bill Clinton, who swept to victory with the slogan: “It’s the economy, stupid”.

Even with Iraq’s armed forces devastated, Saddam was able to frame the military defeat as success: not even a coalition of 42 nations could unseat him. Following huge Republican losses in the 2026 US midterm elections, the Islamic Republic of Iran could claim a similar victory, even with the death of its Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei.

In 2024, Donald Trump ran on an electoral promise of “no more wars”. Two years later, American voters dealt his party a resounding defeat. Not only did Trump begin a war with Iran, but that war is fast becoming another “forever war” with no clear end in sight.

title: Artificial intelligence is desperately seeking its narrative
content:
Since the foundational work of Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter, research has distinguished invention from innovation by its practical implementation. Whether an innovation spreads, however, depends partly on its social acceptance and how its uses are perceived. Without such acceptance, even a promising technology may remain confined to scientific experiments and investors’ speculation. To gain public support, an innovation needs a compelling narrative capable of generating interest, if not enthusiasm. Artificial intelligence illustrates this phenomenon: while its narrative is still taking shape, its social acceptability is increasingly contested.

In July 2026, Le Monde diplomatique declared that “The AI backlash has begun”. The initial sense of wonder generated by ChatGPT has increasingly given way to broader public unease about AI’s social consequences, from its effects on work, education and information to concerns about privacy, the environment and the growing power of technology companies. In this emerging narrative, AI appears as a “digital Moloch” whose costs are borne collectively while its benefits accrue to only a handful of oligarchs.

title: Why young protesters in France are turning against TV channel CNews
content:
On November 5, as secondary school students gathered in Paris for another day of demonstrations, a journalist associated with French media outlet CNews met an unusually hostile reception. Protesters shouted for him to leave, and police officers reportedly asked the journalist to stop heckling the crowd.

What happens when a protest movement turns against the media covering it? In France, students are challenging the government’s education policies and increasingly the news outlets through which their demands reach the public. A petition calling for CNews to be taken off air has gathered more than a million signatures. Petitions and headlines show how much attention the movement commands, but for the protesters themselves, however, the terms of their visibility are part of the problem.

title: Research on migration is going unheard – how can we remedy that?
content:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Policymakers do listen to research, but evidence is only one part of the decision-making process. Public opinion, political pressures, values and competing priorities also shape migration policies.

    • Policymakers do listen to research, but evidence is only one part of the decision-making process. Public opinion, political pressures, values and competing priorities also shape migration policies.

  • How research is communicated matters. Evidence that is presented neutrally can help to build trust among citizens whose concerns and values must also be weighed in the balance.

title: Europe’s protest wave looks like 1968, but the demands are fundamentally different
content:
Spain’s November 11 general strike, called in response to a housing crisis, stagnant wages and rising living costs, is part of a much wider European story. Student-led protests in countries across the continent have spread from schools and universities into broad alliances with trade unions and housing campaigners.

France has seen large-scale unrest, initially linked to conditions in schools. German pupils have mobilised against conscription, thousands have marched in Greece over public education failures, and Serbia’s student protest movement has reshaped its national politics.

The obvious historical parallel is 1968. Then, as now, European student protests spread beyond campuses, crossed borders and drew workers into mass mobilisation. Politicians warned of social breakdown.

This comparison is not wrong. But focusing only on the similarities risks missing an important distinction between the two moments: that the grievances of the protesters are fundamentally different.

title: Don’t wash your laundry at teatime – why planning energy use can reduce your bills
content:
For decades, judging a home’s energy performance meant asking one question: how much does it use? Labels such as energy performance certificates still ask only that.

But homes are changing. Add solar panels, a battery or an electric car, and a house starts to generate, store and sell electricity. Meanwhile, what that electricity costs depends more and more on the clock. Since June 2026, Ireland’s largest suppliers have had to offer tariffs that change every half hour. In the UK, households pay about 26p for each unit they buy, but solar owners can be paid as little as a few pence for each unit they sell.

The question has shifted from how much energy is being used to when is it being consumed? Every building is now an energy system. The clearest example of what that means is a long way from Europe.

In Pakistan, an estimated 7.3 million households, nearly one in five, now have solar panels. In the year to June 2025, panels on homes, shops, farm sheds and small factories produced the equivalent of 46% of all electricity sold through the national grid. Three lessons stand out.

title: AI could transform mathematics, but humans will still need to be in the loop
content:
OpenAI recently announced that one of its AI models solved one of the hardest problems in modern mathematics: the Navier–Stokes problem. The equations at the heart of this problem describe the movement of fluids like water and, according to the scientific definition, air.

The Navier-Stokes equations are essential to understanding phenomena such as ocean currents, blood circulation, and airflow over airplane wings. Yet, mathematicians have struggled for decades to determine whether coherent solutions to these equations exist.

It was for this reason that the US-based Clay Mathematics Institute, which is dedicated to disseminating mathematical knowledge, chose the Navier-Stokes problem as one of its seven Millennium Prize Problems.

These are the most important and challenging unsolved problems in modern mathematics, with a prize of US$1 million (£746,000; €895,000) offered for the first correct solution to each. A problem that resisted generations of mathematicians thus has apparently been solved by artificial intelligence.

title: Why Europe is building both a digital euro and a new mobile payment network
content:
Sending money from your phone seems simple: just choose a contact, enter an amount, and press confirm. But behind these apparently simple actions lie national payment systems that are not always interoperable.

In Europe, the Madrid-based European Network for Payments (ENP) has been established to link five mobile payment solutions operating in 13 European countries: Bizum (Spain), Bancomat (Italy), SIBS-MB WAY (Portugal), Vipps MobilePay (Norway, Denmark, Sweden and Finland) and EPI/Wero (Germany, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Austria).

The combined infrastructure of these organisations covers more than 70% of the population of the EU and Norway, serving a total of around 130 million active users.

The ENP’s rollout will be gradual, beginning with payment between individuals before progressing to online shopping and brick-and-mortar businesses.

But as the EU gets ready to launch the digital euro over the next few years, the question that will spring to mind for many is: Why bother?

title: What the US midterms result means for the Ukraine war
content:
The US midterm elections have shifted the balance of power in Congress, delivering a massive blow to Donald Trump and his Republican party. This has implications both at home and possibly abroad, including for US policy towards Ukraine; an issue that was hardly mentioned during the campaigns.

But even if Ukraine did not figure much in the election, the question in US politics of what to do about the war has not gone away. Indeed, in the weeks and months before the result was announced, Trump had been busily rowing back on US support for Ukraine. This was despite much opposition, even from some Republicans.

Crucial intelligence to Kyiv about Russian strikes was cut off, before later being reinstated, while critical military aid was reduced. Trump also decided to suspend several sanctions on Russia.

This move was denounced by President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine as only helping Russia, but justified by Trump as being “in the national interests of the United States” and also a decision that might help his party’s electoral chances by reducing gas prices.

title: Why Mark Carney is still betting big on Europe
content:
When European Union officials Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa recently joined Mark Carney on the docks of Montréal’s Old Port for the Canada-EU Summit, Canada’s prime minister presented closer ties with the EU as a good deal for Canadian households.

He argued a closer relationship promised more choices and lower costs for families at a time when American tariffs are causing pain on both sides of the Atlantic.

In April 2025, my colleague, Léandre Benoit, and I argued that the newly elected Carney would pursue a pragmatic and globally engaged liberalism, definitively aligned with Europe. The Montréal summit confirms that alignment.

The meeting’s firmest commitments concern democracy, while much of its economic measures are still to be carried out. With autocracies gaining ground around the world, and with Trump’s United States no longer a reliable ally — although that may shift with the Democratic rout in the U.S. midterm elections — Canada and the EU have found in each other stable liberal partners who take democracy seriously.

title: Dementia with Lewy bodies: what you should know about the little-known, progressive brain disease
content:
Robin Williams, Monica Vitti, Patrick Stewart or French actress Nathalie Baye: all these famous people lost their lives to dementia with Lewy bodies.

This neurocognitive disease is only tends to get publicity when a celebrity dies from it. Yet it is a common disease (and one of the most common forms of dementia), in France alone it affects about 250,000 people, which makes it the country’s second most widespread neurodegenerative disease, after Alzheimer’s, putting on a par with Parkinson’s. It is estimated that dementia with Lewy bodies (commonly known as “DLB”) affects more than 10 million patients worldwide.

What causes the disease? What symptoms should we look out for? How is it treated? Here is what you need to know.

Dementia with Lewy bodies owes its name to inclusions that develop inside patients’ neurons called “Lewy bodies”, after the German-born doctor Friedrich Heinrich Lewy, who first discovered their existence in 1912.

However, it was only in 1976 that the first clinical case was formally described, while the first international clinical criteria were defined much later in 1996.

title: The Binance hack exploited familiar weaknesses – all organisations should learn from it
content:
Hackers have stolen around US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, most of which was taken in under an hour. According to Binance, the attack exploited systems and individuals with the authority to carry out transactions involving such large sums.

Such vulnerabilities exist everywhere; statistics show that people and the systems they directly use, including their personal computers, remain a top target for cybercriminals. All organisations could therefore learn lessons from this attack.

The Binance theft took place on the evening of October 29, 2026. The Binance attack netted four times the amount stolen in the previous biggest cryptocurrency theft, on the Bybit exchange in February 2025.

Private keys, used to authorise spending or withdrawal from crypto-wallets, are a known vulnerability. But Binance found no evidence these were leaked. An initial statement from the exchange pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. This gave the attacker access to the internal system that processes withdrawal requests.

title: Speaking in a second language may shift your moral compass – but it can’t overpower it
content:
In today’s interconnected world, millions of people move between two or more languages every day. They may negotiate at work in one language, speak with family in another, and follow news, entertainment and social media across several others.

Using multiple languages can deeply change the way a person sees the world. Research has suggested that thinking and speaking in different languages can fundamentally shift the way we reason and behave, and even change our morality.

Some studies have suggested that using a second language encourages people to make more rational, utilitarian choices, meaning they prioritise the greatest good for the greatest number of people. This is possibly because moral dilemmas feel less emotionally charged when processed in a second language.

But the effect is not cut and dried – other studies have found little or no such effect.

One reason for these mixed findings is that language is only one part of the story. People do not enter a dilemma as a blank slate – they also bring values, past experiences, and sense of self. To date, most research has focused primarily on which language people use, while paying less attention to the person making the decision.

title: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
content:
Donald Trump’s Republican Party has received a stunning rebuke in the US midterm elections. Republicans went into the evening hoping that the polls might be wrong and that they could at least cling on to control of the Senate. But by midnight in Washington, the GOP was staring down what looked like its worst defeat in 50 years.

Republican losses were not just confined to the type of swing districts that parties usually worry about on election night. The scale of the losses was staggering. They lost Senate seats in deep red states such as Texas and South Carolina. They lost districts they had gerrymandered and in which they were supposed to be unbeatable. They lost seats that even the sharpest analysts thought were safe.

Why? For months, surveys have shown that voters are fed up with high prices, with the war in Iran, and with what is increasingly being talked about as the Trump administration’s corruption. A president who was narrowly elected on the promise of a steady economic hand instead spent two years pursuing an extreme ideological agenda favoured only by a minority of Americans. He ignored what voters were saying, and now they have delivered a harsh verdict.

title: ‘National priority’ policies claim to solve Europe’s housing crisis. They may make it worse
content:
Housing shortages and soaring rents are central to Spain’s upcoming general election. As each party presents voters with ways of addressing the crisis, far right party Vox is backing a simple solution: the principle of prioridad nacional, or “national priority”, which would put Spaniards first in line to receive government benefits.

The policy is central to Vox’s programme. It proposes expanding social housing with priority for Spanish nationals, alongside deregulation and tax reductions.

It is presented as a common sense solution, but national priority does not actually address the root causes of scarcity. In fact, it could even make them worse.

The housing crisis, like many crises, has winners as well as losers: while tenants struggle, landlords collect higher rents and enjoy rising asset values. National priority does not change or tackle these underlying inequalities. Instead, it merely ranks neighbours by entitlement to assistance, while also sowing the seeds of social division.

title: From Wales to Finland, minority language speakers still face prejudice
content:
“How very rude to be speaking Welsh.”

That was the complaint a stranger directed at Patsy, a Welsh learner featured in my latest book, after overhearing her family speaking Welsh in a Cardiff cafe. She could hardly believe it: “But you’re in Wales. What are you talking about?”

Wales has come a long way since the days of the Welsh not, a wooden token often accompanied by corporal punishment that was used in some 19th-century schools to discourage children from speaking Welsh. The Welsh language is now more visible, more widely supported and more politically protected than at any point in history.

But my ongoing research of Welsh-speaking families living in Cardiff suggests that while attitudes have improved dramatically, some linguistic prejudice still lingers beneath the surface. The pattern is not unique to Wales. I found similar experiences among Finland’s Swedish-speaking minority, where official recognition of the language has not always translated into acceptance in everyday life.

title: Canada-EU alliance: as a blueprint for a ‘middle-power bloc’ it has a lot of hurdles to overcome
content:
The dream of a Canada-EU “middle-power bloc” has hit its first serious obstacle. At the Montreal summit, Brussels failed to deliver on the promise of associate membership for Canada, despite the enthusiastic backing of European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Instead, the EU offered the hollow consolation of “an ever-closer association”, raising an uncomfortable question about whether the middle powers can overcome their own divisions to become a serious geopolitical force.

The two-day EU-Canada summit culminated on October 30 with the launch of a so-called “Alliance for the Future”. That compromise formula of association, rather than associate membership – which specifically ruled out full membership – was necessary because of internal disagreements in the EU.

In September, Von der Leyen, offered Canada the chance to become the EU’s first “associate member”. But Germany, backed by Greece and others, objected to the term, worried about legal uncertainty and the expectations it might raise in other countries.

title: Stone-age hunters in northern Europe may have used poison arrows to hunt big prey
content:
Autumn walks in Britain are glorious, as the foliage changes colour and cool crisp air begins to bite. However, some of these European trees hide a much darker secret. For example, the lovely red cup-shaped structures on a yew tree, known as arils, conceal seeds that carry dangerous toxins. These toxins may have been used to poison arrow tips in the past.

A new Danish study has shown that the “smoking gun” is not the poison itself, but the size of the small arrowheads used to deliver the toxin into the hunted animal.

The authors of the latest research examined Danish stone tool technology from the period immediately preceding the arrival of farming in Europe – the Mesolithic.

They argue that the distinctive small size of stone arrow tips from the early Mesolithic period (about 9,000–3,950BC) suggest they were used to hunt large prey with the help of poisons. The poison has long since vanished, leaving only the stone tip.

Arrows that do not use poison are typically larger, since they need to damage the animal’s flesh. But poisoned arrows need only wound a prey animal enough to allow the poison to enter the blood stream.

title: Massive sinkholes open up across Turkey as it struggles with drought and climate change
content:
Turkey’s central Anatolian plateau is one of the country’s most important agricultural regions, producing wheat, maize, sugar beet and other crops. Yet beneath its cultivated fields, the ground is becoming increasingly unstable.

Large sinkholes, some tens of metres wide and deep, have appeared across the Konya basin, swallowing farmland, and threatening nearby roads and settlements.

These collapses can occur suddenly, sometimes in fields that have been cultivated for generations. Around 20 are opening up every year, according to a recent study.

Known locally as obruks, sinkholes are not a new geological phenomenon. They have existed in the Konya basin for thousands of years, but they have become far more frequent over recent decades.

Konya’s sinkholes are consequently both a geological hazard and evidence of a wider water-management problem. The cavities beneath the fields are the product of geological processes extending over thousands of years. Their recent instability, however, is occurring within a groundwater system profoundly altered by human activity and increasingly exposed to drought.

title: How the Sphinx is helping answer a riddle about extinct crocodiles
content:
My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza.

Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle.

Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament.

title: Spain’s high-speed train network is plagued by old signalling systems. They may have caused the deadly crash
content:
Shortly after 8am, two high-speed trains set off from Madrid’s Atocha station bound for Seville Santa Justa, but neither reached their destination. A failure in the LZB system – an automatic safety, signalling and protection system that monitors trains’ movement and activates automatic emergency braking – triggered a chain of events that led to a fatal accident, which killed 69 people and left many more injured.

Across the EU’s rail network, which spans almost 227,000km, there are more than 25 different, non-interoperable railway signalling systems. These systems (which include the German LZB, the French Crocodile, the Italian BACC and the Spanish ASFA) control and enable the safe movement of trains via blocks, sections of the track that can only have one train on them at any given moment.

On the Andalusia–Madrid line, the German LZB signalling system remains in operation, pending its replacement by the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) that is already in place on other, more modern lines.

The ERTMS specifications are set out in EU legislation. The aim is for this system to completely replace national ones across the entire EU by 2050.

title: The impossible equation of being a researcher mother, striving to make ends meet
content:
How can we encourage women to pursue scientific careers? In recent years, a number of mentoring or awareness campaigns have been put in place to encourage French high school students to study maths, physics or engineering sciences, while they remain underrepresented in these fields. One of the last large-scale initiatives is the Filles et Maths program, launched in 2025, including work on gender bias, the implementation of “role models” or timetables featuring flexible hours.

The program was nonetheless met with criticism: while women remain under-represented in some disciplines, they also remain a minority in the highest positions across the board in the academic world, from mathematics to social sciences.

In France, gender inequalities are therefore not limited to access to scientific studies: they cut across all university careers and make many women leave French Higher Education and Research before securing tenure. This “drain” is explained by several factors among which motherhood holds an important place. A survey in Denmark illustrates that unlike men, one in three women abandon their scientific career after the birth of their first child.

title: Eurovision 2027: Is Canada singing its way into the European Union?
content:
Officials are meeting this week for the 21st Canada-European Union Leaders’ summit.

It comes only a month after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate membership. A draft statement from Montréal, where Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen and EU Council President António Costa met for two days to discuss strengthening ties, calls for an “ever closer association” that will result “in a more active foreign and security policy partnership.”

The talks follow a series of milestones in the relationship between the transatlantic partners, including the announcement in July that Canada was joining the Eurovision song contest. It’s the first country to do so since Australia entered in 2015.

Eurovision is held every year in May, with member countries submitting one original song. Over the years, the event’s format has changed from an exclusive jury vote to a viewer televote and today’s combination of both.

Sometimes, voting can become political, with viewers voting according to their geopolitical preferences or diaspora communities casting ballots for their former home countries regardless of the quality of the performance.
snippet: Officials are meeting this week for the 21st Canada-European Union Leaders’ summit.
creator: Petra Dolata, Associate Professor, History, University of Calgary

title: Is France in 2026, Greece in 2009?
content:
France’s ten-year government bond yield reached 5% last week, its highest level in more than two decades. The extra interest it pays over Germany – the “spread” investors use to gauge French-specific risk – has widened dramatically. Parliament is wrestling with a 2027 budget requiring €54 billion in fiscal measures, while protests and violent clashes across France dominate the headlines.

With political instability and social tensions rising, comparisons with Greece at the start of its debt crisis have become inevitable. As Greece’s finance minister when its crisis erupted in 2009, I am increasingly asked how the two situations compare. I understand the temptation, but also how misleading it can be.

France is not Greece. It is one of the world’s largest economies, with globally competitive companies, substantial household savings, a deep financial system, robust institutions. And, unlike Greece in 2009, it has no large external financing imbalance.

title: Warmer seas and shifting pressure systems: the signs that suggest the Mediterranean’s climate is ‘tropicalising’
content:
Nowhere in the Iberian Peninsula or the Balearic Islands has a tropical climate – for this to be the case, the average temperature in the coldest month would have to be 18°C or higher. The contrast between Spain’s winters and summers, and the low temperatures reached in winter, do not resemble those of any tropical climate.

However, over recent decades, climates across Mediterranean basin have begun to show signs of tropicalisation: the process of transitioning towards a tropical climate.

This is evident in several areas, including rising air and sea temperatures, shifting atmospheric patterns, and increasingly erratic rainfall.

Firstly, a marked rise in air temperature – more pronounced than the global average – is making the Mediterranean’s winters shorter and its summers longer, bringing spring forward and delaying the onset of autumn. Some people believe that these transitional seasons have all but disappeared. They do still exist, but they have moved on the calendar.

The temperature of shallow and deep Mediterranean water – down to a depth of around 100m – has also risen markedly.

title: Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track
content:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.
snippet: Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.
creator: Guilherme Casarões, Associate Professor of Brazilian Studies, Florida International University
